query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermomechanical treatment—namely, cold rolling with a moderate reduction followed by a subcritical annealing step—will refine the lamellar colony spacing and induce hierarchical nanotwin formation along the dual-phase interfaces, which in turn mitigates dislocation pile-ups, reduces local stress concentrations, and prevents microcracking, thereby overcoming the limited room‐temperature ductility while retaining or increasing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies with relatively coarse internal boundaries that promote dislocation pile-ups, high local stress concentrations, and early microcracking under tensile straining.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled cold-rolling process (e.g., ~50% thickness reduction) followed by a carefully tuned subcritical annealing treatment that does not fully recrystallize the structure but refines the lamellar spacing and nucleates hierarchical nanotwin structures at the colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under quasi-static strain rates. The processing should enforce mechanical deformation at ambient conditions with subsequent heat treatments at temperatures low enough to preserve a dual-phase structure while promoting nanotwin formation.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined ultrafine lamellar microstructure with emergent hierarchical nanotwins along internal boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The refined spacing and the introduction of nanotwins provide additional barriers to dislocation motion in a more distributed manner. This disrupts the formation of dense dislocation pile-ups at each lamellar interface, alleviating local stress concentrations and delaying microcrack initiation. In effect, a more homogeneous plastic flow is promoted, leading to improved ductility without sacrificing, and possibly even enhancing, strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the intervention is predicted to yield significantly higher tensile ductility (i.e., greater elongation to failure) while maintaining or slightly increasing yield and ultimate tensile strengths. However, the magnitude of improvement will depend on the precise processing parameters and initial colony dimensions.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibits brittle behavior at room temperature due to pronounced dislocation pile-ups at relatively coarse internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The proposed improvement is expected to be effective for eutectic high-entropy alloys with similar dual-phase lamellar microstructures. Overprocessing (excessive rolling or annealing) or processing outside the optimal temperature range could lead to either a loss of the beneficial lamellar interfaces or unwanted phase transformations, nullifying the strength–ductility synergy.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative gains in tensile ductility and strength remain uncertain and will depend sensitively on the cold-rolling reduction and annealing conditions. Further optimization is required to validate the parameter window in which nanotwin formation effectively mitigates dislocation pile-ups.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of the eutectic high-entropy alloy. Process each batch with different degrees of cold-rolling reduction (e.g., 30%, 50%, 70%) and follow with a subcritical anneal under controlled conditions. Use TEM and EBSD to evaluate the refinement of lamellar colonies and quantify nanotwin density at the internal interfaces. Subsequently, perform room-temperature tensile tests under identical conditions to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (elongation to failure) across samples.
measurements: Lamellar colony spacing and nanotwin density (via TEM/EBSD)
Dislocation density distribution near internal boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cold-rolled and annealed samples do not exhibit a reproducible and statistically significant increase in tensile ductility (without a loss of strength) compared to the untreated alloy, or if microstructural characterization shows no reduction in dislocation pile-ups (i.e., no notable refinement in lamellar spacing or formation of hierarchical nanotwin structures), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Evading the strength–ductility trade-off dilemma in steel through gradient hierarchical nanotwins

Abstract: The strength–ductility trade-off has been a long-standing dilemma in materials science. This has limited the potential of many structural materials, steels in particular. Here we report a way of enhancing the strength of twinning-induced plasticity steel at no ductility trade-off. After applying torsion to cylindrical twinning-induced plasticity steel samples to generate a gradient nanotwinned structure along the radial direction, we find that the yielding strength of the material can be doubled at no reduction in ductility. It is shown that this evasion of strength–ductility trade-off is due to the formation of a gradient hierarchical nanotwinned structure during pre-torsion and subsequent tensile deformation. A series of finite element simulations based on crystal plasticity are performed to understand why the gradient twin structure can cause strengthening and ductility retention, and how sequential torsion and tension lead to the observed hierarchical nanotwinned structure through activation of different twinning systems. Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
